title: AI Observability Platforms: The Complete 2026 Buyer's Guide (Weave, Braintrust, Arize, Langfuse, Maxim AI, MLflow, Honeycomb Compared)
summary: Compare Weave, Braintrust, Arize, Langfuse, Maxim AI, MLflow, and Honeycomb for AI coding ROI, token spend, engineering output, tracing, and evaluations.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


- **Weave connects AI coding spend and activity to engineering output, quality, and delivery.** It combines developer and tool attribution, complexity-aware output, benchmarks, and model routing.
- **Weave Router provides OTLP traces and routing telemetry** , with a dashboard and export to compatible observability backends.
- Braintrust, Arize, Langfuse, Maxim AI, MLflow, and Honeycomb focus on application and agent tracing or evaluation. Compare products against the engineering or application data your team needs.


## Why "AI observability" means two different things


The products called AI observability platforms serve two distinct use cases. Some monitor LLM requests inside software products, while others measure how engineers use AI coding tools. Production LLM observability follows an individual request through an application. A span records one operation, such as a model response or tool call, while a trace connects those operations into a sequence. Evaluation scores then test the trace for qualities such as accuracy or relevance.[Braintrust](https://www.braintrust.dev/articles/agent-observability-complete-guide-2026) and[Arize Phoenix](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix) collect request-level telemetry that engineers can use to debug agents and LLM applications.


AI coding tool observability aggregates activity across engineers and repositories over time. A platform in this category connects token spend and tool adoption with pull requests, commits, code quality, and delivery metrics.[Weave](https://weaveos.com/) uses those records to examine whether Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or another coding tool changes engineering output. Weave Router adds request-level routing telemetry, while the broader platform connects AI use with engineering work.


The comparison table focuses on four measurements associated with AI coding tools and engineering delivery. Token cost tracking distinguishes per-request model costs from spend across engineering work. Developer-level attribution shows whether usage can be connected to individual engineers. CI/CD integration indicates whether the platform can relate AI activity to code delivery. ROI and benchmarking indicate whether engineering leaders can compare AI-tool adoption and spending with quality, output, and delivery performance. The product profiles assess tracing and evaluation depth separately because those capabilities answer the request-level debugging question.

### Braintrust: connect production traces to evaluations


Braintrust links LLM and tool traces with evaluation datasets and scorers. Its workflow supports comparing changes before release and turning production examples into regression tests. The[vendor guide](https://www.braintrust.dev/articles/best-ai-observability-tools-2026) documents SDK and OpenTelemetry ingestion, cost analysis, and CI evaluations.


Test it with failures from your own application. Check whether your scorers agree with human review and whether your dataset covers common requests and unusual failures. A passing evaluation is evidence about those cases; it does not establish improved engineering delivery.


### Arize Phoenix: inspect runs and test changes on the same inputs


[Phoenix documentation](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix) describes tracing built on OpenTelemetry and OpenInference, evaluations, prompt iteration, datasets, and experiments. Arize also offers the managed AX platform. Compare the edition and deployment you intend to use rather than assuming that every Arize feature is included in Phoenix.


Use a trial to follow a failed request from model call through retrieval and tool use. Then compare a proposed fix on the same dataset. Confirm deployment requirements, retention, and access controls for that edition.


### Langfuse: combine traces, prompts, and evaluation


[Langfuse](https://langfuse.com/docs) brings application traces, prompt versions, experiments, and evaluations into one workflow. Its tracing supports session and user metadata, which can help group application usage and costs. Those identifiers require instrumentation; they do not automatically connect traces to engineering output.


Langfuse also supports[self-hosting](https://langfuse.com/self-hosting) . Compare the operational cost of your chosen deployment with the managed service. Check the current license and edition, storage services, retention controls, and who will maintain the deployment. Do not assume that self-hosting makes the system free to operate.


### Maxim AI: verify the current simulation and evaluation offering


Maxim's[agent quality assurance guide](https://www.getmaxim.ai/articles/ai-agent-quality-assurance-with-maxim-a-comprehensive-guide/) describes scenario simulation, machine and human evaluation, and production tracing. These workflows can help product and engineering teams test conversational behavior and investigate failures before rollout.


The current[Maxim homepage](https://www.getmaxim.ai/) emphasizes Bifrost, an AI gateway. Confirm which simulation and evaluation workflows remain available in the product and plan you are considering. A historical product article establishes what the vendor described; a trial should establish what you can use today.


### MLflow: extend an existing evaluation workflow


[MLflow Tracing](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/genai/tracing/) captures intermediate inputs, outputs, metadata, latency, and token usage. It supports OpenTelemetry ingestion and export, application evaluations, feedback, and datasets built from production examples.


MLflow is useful to evaluate when your team already uses its experiment and model tooling. Check the operational work needed to host it, and compare the open-source deployment with any managed service you are considering. Assess the required capabilities directly rather than assuming production monitoring requires a particular vendor edition.


### Honeycomb: investigate agents within distributed systems


[Honeycomb's agent observability guide](https://www.honeycomb.io/resources/getting-started/agent-observability) applies distributed tracing to agent workflows. This helps teams investigate model requests, tools, and service dependencies together. It is a useful starting point when failures cross application boundaries.


During a trial, reconstruct a real failed request and check whether important steps survive sampling and retention. Also verify the evaluation and feedback workflow you need. Trace visibility explains execution; your quality criteria determine whether the resulting answer or action was useful.


## Run the same acceptance exercise across your shortlist


Use a small set of representative requests, including a failed tool call, a slow response, and an answer that looks correct but fails human review.


1. **Reconstruct the run.** Find the model, prompt version, retrieval steps, tool calls, retries, and error. Record gaps instead of treating a partial trace as complete.
2. **Compare a change.** Run the same inputs before and after a prompt or model update. Keep the scoring criteria fixed and review disagreements with a person who understands the task.
3. **Reconcile costs.** Separate provider billing, token-price estimates, observability charges, and evaluation-model costs. For optimization methods, see our[LLM cost guide](https://weaveos.com/blog/llm-cost-optimization-model-routing-guide) .
4. **Check data controls.** Confirm what prompt and response content is captured, who can access it, and how redaction, export, and deletion work in the selected deployment.
5. **Measure the outcome you bought the tool for.** For an AI application, track successful user tasks and reliability. For coding assistants, connect usage to output, review burden, quality, and delivery using a consistent[AI ROI methodology](https://weaveos.com/methodology/ai-roi) .


Choose a platform when it helps your team answer those questions with its own data. Lower token usage, more traces, or a higher evaluation score alone does not prove better engineering outcomes.

## Combining the two categories


Production tracing and coding-tool observability can operate together because they measure different activity. Application and ML owners can use Braintrust, Arize Phoenix, Langfuse, Maxim AI, MLflow, or Honeycomb to inspect agent behavior, while engineering leaders can use[Weave](https://weaveos.com/) to assess coding-tool adoption, spending, and delivery outcomes.


Start with a tracing platform when you need to inspect production requests. When you need to assess spending on Claude Code, Cursor, or Codex, consider how[Weave](https://weaveos.com/) connects usage data with engineering outcomes.

## FAQs


**Is LLM observability the same as AI observability?**


LLM observability tracks prompts, responses, tool calls, latency, cost, and evaluation scores for AI applications. Weave covers a different use of AI observability by connecting coding-tool usage and token spend to engineering outcomes. Separating these categories helps you choose tools based on the data you need.


**Can I use Braintrust and Weave together?**


Braintrust and Weave measure separate parts of AI-enabled software development. Braintrust traces production agents, while Weave relates AI coding-tool activity to code quality, delivery, and spend. Using both gives application engineers request-level trace data and engineering leaders aggregated coding-tool outcome data.


**What does agent observability track that engineering observability does not?**


Agent observability records the steps an AI agent takes during an individual request, including model calls, retrievals, tool use, errors, and evaluations. Weave connects usage across developers, repositories, and delivery workflows, and Weave Router also exposes request-level routing traces. Agent traces help application engineers debug individual requests, while aggregated usage data helps engineering leaders assess adoption and delivery outcomes.


**Which AI observability tools support self-hosting?**


Self-hosted LLM observability keeps trace and evaluation data on infrastructure you control. Arize Phoenix, Langfuse, and MLflow provide open-source self-hosting options, and Weave Router supports self-hosted deployment with OTLP telemetry. Self-hosting can support data residency requirements, but you must operate the required storage and services.
